01 — Interaction Design, UOC

Atlas

My first assumption was that people don't document their trips well enough. The interviews corrected that fast — people already photograph and note things down constantly. What gets lost happens afterward, once those memories sit unopened in a camera roll.

Atlas was built to fix that second part, not the first.

View prototype in Figma View design file Report

Home — the current trip always visible, with recent activities listed right below.

An unexpected finding

I built two personas, Sofía and Mateo, assuming they'd represent different user types. The card sorting session showed something more useful: both of them, independently, split "my current trip" from "all my past trips" into two separate mental categories.

That's when I stopped designing what felt intuitive to me and started designing around what they were already doing, unprompted.

The actual card sorting session: the groups that emerged without me suggesting them.

The riskiest call

  • Putting the "add memory" button at the center of the bottom bar, as the primary action, was the decision I second-guessed the most. But the research was clear: if capturing something takes more than one tap, people don't do it. I chose a slightly bolder layout over one nobody would actually use.
  • Registering a memory isn't one screen, it's a stack of layers. The goal was to never make it feel like you'd left what you were doing just to save something.

What the test confirmed (and what didn't go perfectly)

All four tasks were completed without anyone getting stuck. The flow I took the biggest risk on — quick memory registration — was also the one the tester finished fastest and most naturally.

One thing did come up: on the preview screen, she asked "can I tap this?" about an element that was interactive but didn't look like it. A small issue, and worth noting precisely because it's small.

02 — Design Management, UOC

Lufe

Lufe was already doing a lot right: 7x revenue growth in five years, 377K followers, a community that trusts the brand enough to buy furniture without ever touching it first. That last part was both its biggest strength and its clearest weak point.

View full dossier

Why I ruled out two full proposals

I designed three possible directions and presented all three, not just the one I picked, because explaining why something shouldn't be built is as much part of the job as proposing what should. One option was too cautious to move the needle. The other was too ambitious for a 48-person company that didn't yet have the structure to support it.

The one that holds up: Lufe Studio

A 3D configurator to solve the one problem nobody had addressed — seeing the furniture before buying it — a loyalty program that turns buyers into a community, and a TikTok strategy that doesn't invent anything new, just structures what Lufe already did well.

All of it scoped into two-week sprints, with something testable on real users from month one.

03 — Editorial Design, UOC

Sal

SAL is about chefs who gave up technical perfection for something more honest, and less comfortable. I wanted the magazine itself to work the same way — no decoration for its own sake. Every bit of white space, every page break, had to earn its place.

View full magazine

A system you don't notice until it's gone

A six-column grid, one red as the only accent, nothing else competing for attention. Fraunces for impact, Syne for reading without fatigue. If something drew attention without a reason, it came out.

Designing the pace, not just the page

The opening hits with a full-bleed photo. The next page breathes with a standalone quote on a colored background. And the close slows you down in a narrow column, as if the text itself were asking for patience. That sequence wasn't incidental — it was the plan from the first sketch.

04 — Brand Identity, UOC

ArteCódigo

The brand is fictional. The process behind it isn't. "Where art meets code" only works as an idea if every visual choice picks a side — organic or systematic — or mixes them on purpose. There's no accidental middle ground.

Building a logo like it's code

An 8×8 module grid, as rigid as any digital design system. Two typefaces speak for the two worlds the brand merges: Anonymous Pro, technical and monospaced, for the logotype; Roboto Mono, easier to read, for everything else.

Taking the system into the real world

A brand manual only proves something if it survives outside the PDF — on a tote bag, on an "Exit" sign, on a storefront. Here are those three tests.

05 — HTML & CSS, UOC

Nexus

Four pages for a fictional digital agency, hand-coded from a design that was already provided: home, services, about and contact. The challenge wasn't inventing the interface, it was building it with semantic HTML5 and well-organized CSS that meets WCAG AA accessibility, point by point — from color contrast to the skip-navigation link.

View live site

Home — the agency's hero section, condensed type and the lime accent setting the pace.

Accessible beyond what you can see

A hidden skip-navigation link that only appears on keyboard focus. Every form field has a properly associated label and a visible focus state, and required fields are marked in a way a screen reader can actually detect, not just a colored asterisk.

Actually semantic HTML

The pricing table uses a proper caption and column headers, not a grid built out of divs. Every section is tied to its own heading, and each page declares its language and title correctly. None of this changes how the page looks. It changes who can use it.

About me

I'm studying Design and Digital Creation at UOC, moving toward product without rushing the steps in between. What keeps me interested in design isn't mostly the visual side — though I like that too — it's the point where a decision stops being "I like it better this way" and becomes "this works better for this specific reason."

I'm still learning something new most weeks, and I'd rather that show up in the work than on a resume.
